sections.h2: Which sale route fits an Orlando house on a timeline?
sections.html:
Orlando sellers can accept a cash offer, hire an agent or sell directly, and the best fit turns on how much work the house needs and whether a historic district rule covers the address. Orlando had an estimated 333,888 residents in July 2025, and its housing stock ranges from downtown condos to bungalows built in the 1920s.

  • Cash offers suit houses with deferred repairs, tenant trouble or a tight deadline, since no lender stands between you and closing.
  • A traditional listing suits a house in good condition that can take several rounds of showings.
  • A direct sale suits an owner who already has a buyer lined up, such as a neighbor or a tenant.

Before choosing, find out whether your street sits inside one of the city's six historic preservation districts, because that changes what the next owner can do to the exterior.

sections.h2: How many Orlando homes are owner-occupied, and what do they cost?
sections.html:
Renters outnumber owners in Orlando: Census Bureau figures for 2020-2024 give owners only 39.5% of homes. Landlords and investors are therefore a regular part of the buyer pool, and many sellers own rental houses.

sections.h2: How did Orlando's lakes and old neighborhoods take shape?
sections.html:
The city's own Lake Eola history says Jacob Summerlin bought 200 acres in what is now Downtown Orlando in 1873, and a sinkhole on the edge of the property filled into the lake first known as Sandy Beach. The Summerlin family donated land around the shore in 1883, and in 1888 Lake Eola became a public park.

The preservation districts tell the next chapter. Land north of the lake was planted in citrus until the freezes of 1894 and 1895 devastated the groves, after which it was subdivided for homes, and Lake Eola Heights grew most between 1905 and 1925. Colonialtown South was platted in part in 1883, and most of its houses went up during the 1920s land boom. Houses from those eras are common sale listings, and their age is why the local rules below matter.

sections.h2: Does a historic district change how I sell an Orlando house?
sections.html:
It can, since a house in one of Orlando's six local historic preservation overlay districts needs city approval before exterior changes. The city's Orlando Locator, which takes an address, shows whether you live in a district. Most districts require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic Preservation Board, while the Downtown Historic District uses a Certificate of Appearance Approval from the Appearance Review Board.

  • Major work such as additions, new construction, relocation and demolition goes to a board hearing, and the city says to expect about seven weeks.
  • Lake Eola Heights does not require approval for landscaping, paint color, or patios and walkways out of public view.
  • In Lake Copeland, approval is not needed for work that needs no city building permit or for structures built after January 1, 1940.
  • Chain-link fencing is restricted in Lake Eola Heights and Lake Lawsona.

The city also reports that on August 10, 2026 the City Council approved a 36-month temporary change that moves reviews of new or renovated downtown projects from the Historic Preservation Board to the Appearance Review Board. For questions, the Historic Preservation Officer line is 407.246.3416, and Permitting is 407.246.2271.

sections.h2: Is there a tax break that stays with a historic Orlando house?
sections.html: Yes, for rehabilitated historic property. Orlando adopted a property tax exemption in 1994 for the substantial rehabilitation of locally designated historic property. It runs 10 years and covers 100 percent of the city's share of the tax tied to the value added by the rehabilitation, and the city says the exemption stays intact when the property sells. If your house has had that work done, mention it in the listing and keep the paperwork for the buyer.

sections.h2: What happens to my homestead tax benefits when I sell?
sections.html:
Orange County's property appraiser says homestead can reduce taxable value by up to $50,000, and the office posts a tax estimator tool meant for people planning to buy or sell. Bills arrive each November, and paying that month earns the largest early-payment discount.

Your homestead ends at sale. The next owner files their own by March 1, and the property is reassessed at just value, a reset that follows any sale, foreclosure or transfer of title, with exceptions for spouses and certain transfers at death. Buying again in Florida? Portability can move part of your capped assessment to the new home if you establish it within three years.

Older owners and veterans may hold added breaks that the buyer will not inherit. A local ordinance can give people 65 and older an extra exemption of up to $50,000 within an income limit, and a veteran with a permanent service-connected disability may receive a discount matching the VA rating. Ask the property appraiser what applies to you.

sections.h2: Which closing charge hits the Orlando deed?
sections.html: The state's deed tax is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and the Department of Revenue lists all counties except Miami-Dade at that rate. Every party to the deed is liable for the tax whoever agrees to pay it in the contract, and the clerk collects it at recording. Clerk recording charges start at $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, with added per-name and technology charges. Your closing agent will show the total.

sections.h2: What if a tenant is living in the house I am selling?
sections.html: A tenant in place shapes your timeline. Florida requires 60 days' notice to end a year-to-year tenancy, and the sheriff gives 24 hours of posted notice before returning possession once a court rules for the landlord. Many investors buy occupied houses, so a lease is not always an obstacle, and the buyer can take the house with the tenant in it.

faqs.q: How can I tell whether my address is in a historic district?
faqs.a: Enter your address in the Orlando Locator on the city's website, or call the city's Historic Preservation Officer at 407.246.3416. Six local districts exist: Downtown, Lake Cherokee, Lake Copeland, Lake Eola Heights, Lake Lawsona and Colonialtown South.

faqs.q: How long do Orlando's historic approvals run?
faqs.a: Minor work can clear a quick review in 2 to 10 days in most districts and 10 to 15 days downtown. Major work needs a board hearing, and the city says to expect about seven weeks from the closing date of the application.

faqs.q: Does my Save Our Homes cap pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. A sale is a change of ownership, so the county returns the property to just value. The buyer applies for a fresh homestead by March 1 if they live there on January 1.

faqs.q: What is the stamp tax on a deed in Orange County?
faqs.a: The rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, collected by the clerk when the deed is recorded. Miami-Dade is the only county with a different structure. Ask the closing agent for the exact amount on your deed.

faqs.q: Can an inherited Orlando house be sold quickly?
faqs.a: Often, once the estate has authority to sell. Florida offers a simplified summary administration for some smaller or older estates, and creditor claims have their own cutoff dates. A probate attorney can confirm which path your estate takes.
